deep.reconstruction:
This page contains no derivation. It is a prose draft, probably the opening of a lecture or exposition labelled 'Riemann 26', on Gauss's theory of terrestrial magnetism and the observing programme of the Göttingen Magnetic Union (Magnetischer Verein, about 1834 to 1841). The previous page, on oscillation period and damping of a magnet bar, fits the same context: Gauss–Weber instruments.

Content, step by step:
(1) The founding of the Magnetic Union for the study of terrestrial magnetism by Gauss, and his instructions for observations on the fixed 'Termine' (simultaneous observation dates), are called an epoch-making event in mathematical as well as experimental physics.
(2) Definition. The terrestrial magnetic force is postulated to explain an observed fact. A magnetic needle suspended at its centre of gravity and free to swing takes a definite direction at every place on the Earth's surface. When displaced, it is driven back by a definite force (restoring torque). It is called 'erdmagnetisch' because it is explained by assuming that the Earth is a magnet.
(3) Gauss's 'Allgemeine Theorie des Erdmagnetismus' (1839) rests only on one hypothesis. The force is the resultant of the actions of all magnetic particles of the Earth. Each particle acts at a distance by Coulomb's law: force proportional to 1/r^2, repulsive between like and attractive between unlike poles. In modern terms (my gloss): the field is B = -grad V, where V is a superposition of 1/r potentials, hence harmonic outside the Earth. It therefore has an expansion in solid spherical harmonics, V = a * sum_n (a/r)^(n+1) * sum_m P_n^m(cos theta) (g_n^m cos m*lambda + h_n^m sin m*lambda).
(4) The general laws that follow from this hypothesis are the relations between the forces at different points of the Earth's surface. These relations were fully confirmed by experience (Gauss's fit with 24 coefficients up to degree 4).
(5) The significance for mathematical physics: this was the first case where the great progress made since the end of the 18th century in following the states of an extended body in detail was put to practical use. Here Riemann means potential theory and the analysis of continua (Laplace, Legendre, Poisson). The text breaks off at 'In der That, bei einem ...'.

No computations to reconstruct.

results.what: Gauss's general theory of terrestrial magnetism: the field is derived from a potential of inverse-square (Coulomb) magnetic elements, giving relations between field components at different surface points (spherical harmonic analysis).
results.modern_name: Gauss spherical-harmonic (potential) representation of the geomagnetic field
results.usually_credited_to: C. F. Gauss, Allgemeine Theorie des Erdmagnetismus (1839)

results.what: Historical assessment: Gauss's geomagnetism as the first practical application of the potential theory of extended bodies developed since the late 18th century.
results.modern_name: History of potential theory / geomagnetism (expository remark)

deep.surprise_reason: This is a lecture-style historical and expository introduction to Gauss's well-known theory of terrestrial magnetism, with no new mathematics. Riemann's close association with Gauss and Weber and his work on physics lectures make such a draft entirely expected.

checkable.asserts: The Coulomb (1/r) potential of a magnetic element is harmonic away from the source, the basis of Gauss's potential theory.
The force from the 1/r potential has magnitude inversely proportional to the square of the distance (Coulomb's law).
The dipole potential (the leading term of Gauss's expansion) is harmonic outside the Earth.
